title: The Vertigo of Being Promoted Past My Competence
script: Narrator: [measured] There's a particular vertigo that arrives roughly six months into a promotion you privately suspect exceeded your actual capabilities, a suspicion no congratulatory email quite manages to dispel.
Narrator: [honest] I'd spent a decade excelling at the discrete, bounded work of an individual contributor, the kind with visible edges and defensible outcomes.
Narrator: [reflective] Leadership, by contrast, offered no such edges, only an amorphous expectation that I somehow metabolize other people's ambiguity into decisions nobody else wanted to own.

Narrator: [uneasy] I performed competence for months, nodding through meetings whose stakes I only half grasped, terrified that admitting confusion would confirm what I already suspected everyone secretly believed.
Narrator: [thoughtful] The exhaustion of that performance eventually outpaced my capacity to sustain it, which is, I've since realized, precisely how most people finally confess to struggling.
Narrator: [honest] I told my own mentor, haltingly, that I thought the promotion had been a mistake, that I'd been elevated past whatever ceiling my actual skill honestly warranted.

Narrator: [reflective] She didn't reassure me, which I initially resented, and instead asked a question I hadn't thought to ask myself: whether competence at this level even resembled competence at the last one.

Narrator: [analytical] It doesn't, I slowly understood. The very qualities that had made me exceptional before, precision, individual ownership, a taste for solving things alone, actively undermined me now.
Narrator: [thoughtful] What this role actually demanded was closer to translation than execution: absorbing chaos from a dozen directions and returning something coherent enough for others to act on.
Narrator: [determined] So I stopped measuring myself against my old competence entirely, and began, awkwardly, building the unfamiliar muscles this altogether different job actually required.
Narrator: [warmly] The vertigo hasn't disappeared completely, and I suspect it never fully will, each new altitude apparently arriving with its own particular thinness of air.
Narrator: [peacefully] But I've stopped mistaking that thinness for proof I don't belong here, and started treating it, instead, as the unglamorous, ordinary texture of actually growing.

quiz.question: When does the narrator say this vertigo typically arrives?
options: Immediately after the promotion
Roughly six months into a promotion he privately suspects exceeded his capabilities
Only on his last day
Before the promotion was even announced
quiz.explanation: He says the vertigo arrives about six months in, once the initial congratulations fade.

quiz.question: What kind of work had the narrator excelled at previously?
options: Vague, unstructured leadership tasks
Discrete, bounded individual-contributor work with visible edges and defensible outcomes
Public speaking engagements
Managing large teams
quiz.explanation: He had excelled at bounded individual-contributor work with clear edges, unlike the ambiguity of leadership.

quiz.question: What question did his mentor ask instead of reassuring him?
options: Whether he wanted to quit
Whether competence at this level even resembled competence at the last one
Whether he had asked for a raise
Whether his team liked him
quiz.explanation: His mentor asked whether competence at his new level even resembled competence at his previous one, prompting reflection.

quiz.question: What did the narrator realize his old strengths did in the new role?
options: They transferred perfectly
They actively undermined him, since the role demanded different qualities
They were completely irrelevant either way
They made the promotion easier
quiz.explanation: He realized the precision and solo focus that once made him excellent now actively undermined him in the new role.

quiz.question: How does the narrator ultimately interpret the persistent 'thinness of air'?
options: As proof he doesn't belong in the role
As the unglamorous, ordinary texture of actually growing
As a sign he should resign immediately
As something that will vanish completely soon
quiz.explanation: He stops treating the vertigo as proof of not belonging and instead treats it as the ordinary texture of growth.
